power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.title: Non-Significant P Value Check
stat_p_nonsig.summary_text: We found 2 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

table.formatted: With the FPR gap it was 0.28 (p = 0.072), and with the AUROC drop 0.72 (Figure <ref type="figure">5</ref>).
table.expanded: With the FPR gap it was 0.28 (p = 0.072), and with the AUROC drop 0.72 (Figure 5).

table.formatted: Within attributes the correlation with the TPR gap was 0.74 for sex (interval 0.19 to 0.94 when encoders are resampled, p < 0.001) and 0.19 for age (-0.29 to 0.57, p = 0.417), so the relation was clear across encoders for sex and uncertain within age.
table.expanded: Within attributes the correlation with the TPR gap was 0.74 for sex (interval 0.19 to 0.94 when encoders are resampled, p < 0.001) and 0.19 for age (-0.29 to 0.57, p = 0.417), so the relation was clear across encoders for sex and uncertain within age.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = 0.072", "p = 0.417"), Sentence = c("With the FPR gap it was 0.28 (p = 0.072), and with the AUROC drop 0.72 (Figure 5).", "Within attributes the correlation with the TPR gap was 0.74 for sex (interval 0.19 to 0.94 when encoders are resampled, p < 0.001) and 0.19 for age (-0.29 to 0.57, p = 0.417), so the relation was clear across encoders for sex and uncertain within age." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

#### Unclassified Files

We could not classify 3 files by name or extension: .gitattributes, Dockerfile, meta_model.joblib. Add a recognisable keyword (`data`, `code`, `materials`, `documentation`, `output`) to the file name, or use a common extension, so both humans and machines can tell what kind of file it is.
#### File Naming

File names should be machine-parseable: no spaces or special characters, and every file should be classifiable by name or extension. We found 3 naming problems that should be fixed, and 0 files with a naming suggestion (not required, but a good habit).
#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 1 file that software creates by itself, not the authors: editor settings (1). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 38 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

#### Reported vs. reproduced
28 statistical tests reported in the manuscript text were checked against the extracted analysis output: 2 matched (2 fully, 0 partially) — 7.1% found.
Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). The "Plausible" column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output's own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.

text.text: Background and Objective: A classifier trained on frozen embeddings can take a shortcut through a sensitive attribute only if the embedding carries information about it beyond what the task label explains: its shortcut potential.
We asked whether this can be measured on the embedding alone with a known false positive rate, and whether it predicts how strongly a classifier trained on confounded data relies on the attribute.
Methods: ShortKit-ML tests whether an embedding E and a sensitive attribute A are dependent given a task label Y .
The primary test is a conditional probe: a logistic regression that predicts A from E and Y , scored by out-of-fold AUROC and calibrated by permuting A within levels of Y , between patients.
Five secondary detectors share this null.
We audited sex, age

Deep learning models for medical imaging can reach expert-level accuracy on many diagnostic tasks, including skin cancer classification [1] and pneumonia detection on chest radiographs [2], as well as breast cancer screening [3].
text.formatted: Deep learning models for medical imaging can reach expert-level accuracy on many diagnostic tasks, including skin cancer classification <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> and pneumonia detection on chest radiographs <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>, as well as breast cancer screening <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: High accuracy does not show that a model uses clinically meaningful evidence.
Models often rely on shortcuts: signals that predict the label in the training data but are not part of the clinical mechanism, and that stop working when the data change [4].
text.formatted: Models often rely on shortcuts: signals that predict the label in the training data but are not part of the clinical mechanism, and that stop working when the data change <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: In medical imaging, chest drains have served as proxies for pneumothorax [5], while pneumonia models have learned the hospital a radiograph came from [6] and hip fracture models have drawn on scanner and patient variables [7].
text.formatted: In medical imaging, chest drains have served as proxies for pneumothorax <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>, while pneumonia models have learned the hospital a radiograph came from <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> and hip fracture models have drawn on scanner and patient variables <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Patient race can be recognised from chest radiographs [8], and organ segmentation models show biases linked to sex, age and scanner manufacturer [9].
text.formatted: Patient race can be recognised from chest radiographs <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>, and organ segmentation models show biases linked to sex, age and scanner manufacturer <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: each level of Y , which is the single primary test (Section 3).
Five secondary detectors rewritten to score the attribute within task strata and calibrated by the same null, so that every reported p-value has a known false positive rate.
A synthetic benchmark in which A and Y are separate variables and the true answer is known, with linear, nonlinear and variance-shift signals (Section 4.1).

Audits of seven frozen encoders on CheXpert and four on MIMIC-CXR (Section 4.2), and a classification-head experiment on CheXpert that tests whether the measured potential predicts reliance on the attribute by a head trained on confounded data, and whether four mitigation methods reduce that reliance (Section 4.3).

An open package in which every table, figure and result number of this paper is regenerated by committed scripts from runs whose manifests record the code commit, the configuration and hashes of the inputs, with two integrity checks, a fake patient-level attribute and a rowalignment check between encoders, that caught faults in our own data (Appendix F).
The package also contains methods that need model training, gradients or concept examples.
They are documented, but they are outside the audit score evaluated here (Section 3.5).
Shortcut learning in medical imaging.
Geirhos et al. defined shortcut learning as reliance on decision rules that work on the training distribution but fail to transfer [4].
text.formatted: Geirhos et al. defined shortcut learning as reliance on decision rules that work on the training distribution but fail to transfer <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Texture bias in ImageNet classifiers [21] and annotation artefacts in natural language inference [22] are early examples, and recent surveys give taxonomies of dataset bias [23] and of spurious correlations [24].
text.formatted: Texture bias in ImageNet classifiers <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> and annotation artefacts in natural language inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> are early examples, and recent surveys give taxonomies of dataset bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> and of spurious correlations <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref>.

text.text: Medical examples include site-specific signal in pneumonia detection that degraded external performance [6] and scanner and hospital process variables in hip fracture prediction [7].
text.formatted: Medical examples include site-specific signal in pneumonia detection that degraded external performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> and scanner and hospital process variables in hip fracture prediction <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Other documented shortcuts are slide-origin signal in pathology [25], chest drains [26] and laterality markers [27] in radiography, and rulers in dermoscopy [28].
text.formatted: Other documented shortcuts are slide-origin signal in pathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>, chest drains <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref> and laterality markers <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref> in radiography, and rulers in dermoscopy <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref>.

text.text: Reviews in radiology catalogue these routes [29, 30].
text.formatted: Reviews in radiology catalogue these routes <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30]</ref>.

text.text: Hill et al. trained models on knee radiographs to predict targets that should not be visible, such as whether a patient drinks beer, and reached above-chance AUROC through sex, site and scanner signals that preprocessing did not remove [12].
text.formatted: Hill et al. trained models on knee radiographs to predict targets that should not be visible, such as whether a patient drinks beer, and reached above-chance AUROC through sex, site and scanner signals that preprocessing did not remove <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: Encoding of protected attributes.
Gichoya et al. showed that deep models recognise self-reported race from chest radiographs with high accuracy, and that the signal survives image degradation [8].
text.formatted: Gichoya et al. showed that deep models recognise self-reported race from chest radiographs with high accuracy, and that the signal survives image degradation <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Glocker et al. found that chest X-ray disease detection models encode sex and race but appear to make little use of them for disease prediction [11], and that classifiers built on the frozen features of a chest radiography foundation model show subgroup performance gaps [31].
text.formatted: Glocker et al. found that chest X-ray disease detection models encode sex and race but appear to make little use of them for disease prediction <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>, and that classifiers built on the frozen features of a chest radiography foundation model show subgroup performance gaps <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref>.

text.text: Jones et al. showed that subgroup separability, how well the group can be recovered from the image, governs how much a group's performance degrades when its labels are biased [32], and argued that the right mitigation depends on the causal structure of the bias [33].
text.formatted: Jones et al. showed that subgroup separability, how well the group can be recovered from the image, governs how much a group's performance degrades when its labels are biased <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref>, and argued that the right mitigation depends on the causal structure of the bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref>.

text.text: Yang et al. reported that models which encode more demographic information show larger fairness gaps, and that removing the information does not always help on external data [34]. Brown et al. addressed the step between encoding and use directly: shortcut testing varies how strongly a model encodes an attribute and measures the effect on fairness, which separates attributes that are used from attributes that are only present [10]. Petersen et al. argued that a demographically invariant representation is neither necessary nor sufficient for a fair model, and that a representation carrying only disease-relevant features will correlate with group whenever those features do [13].
text.formatted: Yang et al. reported that models which encode more demographic information show larger fairness gaps, and that removing the information does not always help on external data <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref>. <ref type="bibr">Brown et al. addressed</ref> the step between encoding and use directly: shortcut testing varies how strongly a model encodes an attribute and measures the effect on fairness, which separates attributes that are used from attributes that are only present <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>. <ref type="bibr">Petersen et al.</ref> argued that a demographically invariant representation is neither necessary nor sufficient for a fair model, and that a representation carrying only disease-relevant features will correlate with group whenever those features do <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: Kina and Petersen trained pneumothorax classifiers with chest drains as a confounded shortcut, on finetuned and frozen foundation-model encoders, and found that recalibrating the head separately for each shortcut group, with the representation unchanged, recovered much of the performance on images where drain and label disagree [14].
text.formatted: Kina and Petersen trained pneumothorax classifiers with chest drains as a confounded shortcut, on finetuned and frozen foundation-model encoders, and found that recalibrating the head separately for each shortcut group, with the representation unchanged, recovered much of the performance on images where drain and label disagree <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: On frozen encoders, then, much of shortcut use is decided in the head.
Our audit sits at the encoding step, and the head experiment tests whether the encoded signal gets used.
Probing and dependence measures.
Probes were introduced to read what a layer represents [17] and are now a standard tool, with known caveats about probe capacity and what a high probe score means [18].

text.text: Bolukbasi et al. removed a gender direction from word embeddings [35].

text.text: Let E ∈ R n×d be embeddings of n images from a frozen encoder, where Y denotes the task label and A is a sensitive attribute with G groups.
The
Table 1: Comparison of existing bias and shortcut detection tools.
Footnotes define the entries in the Embedding analysis and Multi-method columns.
audit tests the null hypothesis which holds exactly when the conditional mutual information I(E; A | Y ) is zero.
In words, the audit asks whether the embedding holds any information about the attribute that the task label does not already account for.
If H 0 holds, a classifier trained on E to predict Y cannot gain anything from A beyond its correlation with Y , so the shortcut potential is zero.
Rejecting H 0 shows only that the potential is positive.
Whether a particular head uses it is tested separately in Section 4.3.
Conditioning on Y matters: if A and Y are correlated, an embedding that encodes only Y will also predict A, and an unconditional test would flag it.
The tests in this paper are linear, so they have power against dependence that shifts the mean of E between groups of A within Y .
Section 5.1 shows that they have none against signals that leave those means unchanged.
A positive result reads differently when the attribute has physical correlates in the image.
Sex, for example, is associated with chest anatomy, so a positive audit for sex is expected and may be clinically harmless.

The audit reports only that the information is there, since an anatomical correlate and an unwanted one are both dependence between E and A given Y , and it leaves that judgement, and the head experiment, to the analyst.

Each detector m returns a continuous statistic s m (E, A, Y ), where larger means more information about A in E. Calibration asks how large that statistic would be if the embedding carried no information about the attribute beyond the task label, and answers this by recomputing it on data where that is true by construction.
To build such data, we permute A within each stratum of Y , which keeps the joint distribution of (A, Y ) and of (E, Y ) but breaks any dependence between E and A given Y [39].
text.formatted: To build such data, we permute A within each stratum of Y , which keeps the joint distribution of (A, Y ) and of (E, Y ) but breaks any dependence between E and A given Y <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[39]</ref>.

text.text: When a cohort has several images per patient, the attribute is constant within a patient, so we permute it between patients within three strata (all of a patient's images negative for the task, all positive, or mixed) and keep all images of a patient together in the cross-validation folds.

On CheXpert with Pneumothorax as the task these strata hold 421, 12 and 44 of the 477 patients, so in the stratified permutation no patient is without a partner; in the labelled-only subsets of Section 4.3 and in the test halves audited after mitigation the smallest stratum held 4 patients.

Patients in one stratum are treated as exchangeable, which assumes that their number of images and, in the mixed stratum, their share of positive images are unrelated to A. On CheXpert neither quantity differed by sex or by age (Mann-Whitney p from 0.55 to 0.83 over the 4 comparisons, 44 mixed patients).

An attribute that can differ between images of one patient, such as the planted marker, is permuted in blocks: whole patients' attribute vectors are exchanged between patients with the same task labels and number of images.
In the block permutation of the planted-marker audit, 449 of the 477 patients had at least one such partner.
The 28 without one keep their observed vector in every permutation, which leaves the test valid and only reduces the number of distinct permutations.
Repeating this K times gives null statistics s (1) m , . . . , s (K) m and the permutation p-value which is valid at any sample size [50].
text.formatted: Repeating this K times gives null statistics s (1) m , . . . , s (K) m and the permutation p-value which is valid at any sample size <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">[50]</ref>.

text.text: Under H 0 , and when A is exchangeable within the strata, every detector then has false positive rate at most α, whatever its scale or dimensionality.
The observed rates on synthetic null data are given in Table 2 and Section 5.1.
text.formatted: The observed rates on synthetic null data are given in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">2</ref> and Section 5.1.

text.text: We use K = 500 for the probe in the clinical audits and the head experiment, and K = 200 for the secondary statistics, the synthetic grid and the audits after mitigation (Appendix D).
Within one audit cell (one embedding, attribute and task), the conditional probe is the single primary test and is judged at its own level, p < 0.05.
text.formatted: Within one audit cell (one embedding, attribute and task), the conditional probe is the single primary test and is judged at its own level, p < 0.05.

text.text: The p-values of the five secondary detectors are adjusted by the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure [51] across those five, and a secondary detector is flagged when its adjusted value q m < 0.05.
text.formatted: The p-values of the five secondary detectors are adjusted by the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">[51]</ref> across those five, and a secondary detector is flagged when its adjusted value q m < 0.05.

text.text: Earlier versions of the package compared each statistic against a fixed threshold, such as probe accuracy above 70%.
Those thresholds are no longer used for any decision.
The primary test is a conditional probe.

The idea is that if a linear classifier predicts the attribute from the embedding and the task label better than it could from the task label alone, the embedding carries attribute information that the task label does not explain.
An L2-regularised logistic regression predicts A from the standardised embedding concatenated with Y .
Its score is the out-of-fold AUROC from 5-fold cross-validation stratified on (A, Y ) and grouped by patient where patient identifiers exist.
When G > 2 it is macro-averaged over one binary one-vs-rest regression per group, and in every case it is averaged over five random fold splits.
text.formatted: When G > 2 it is macro-averaged over one binary one-vs-rest regression per group, and in every case it is averaged over five random fold splits.

text.text: Standardisation is fitted inside each training fold, and Y enters as one more standardised column under the same penalty (every task here is binary).

Each permuted data set uses a single fold split, which makes the test slightly conservative (the permuted score has the same expectation as the observed five-split average but more variance, so the null is wider), and the fold splits come from a random stream separate from the permutations, so the observed score does not depend on K. Across fold splits the score had an SD of at most 0.018 on CheXpert and 0.013 on MIMIC-CXR.
The regularisation strength is C = 1.
Because Y is an input, the probe can reach an AUROC above 0.5 from Y alone when A and Y are correlated.
The permuted data keep that correlation, so the null distribution absorbs it and only the information that E adds is tested.

For the same reason the AUROC is pooled over the Y strata rather than computed within each: pooling raises the null mean when A and Y are correlated, and under H 0 it raises the observed score by the same amount.

Along with the probe AUROC and its permutation p-value, we report a 95% confidence interval from 2000 bootstrap resamples of patients (identities on CelebA) applied to the out-of-fold predictions, which does not include the variation between fold splits reported above.
We chose a linear probe so that a positive result means the attribute is linearly available to a linear head, which is how frozen embeddings are usually used.
Five secondary detectors are reported with their continuous scores and calibrated p-values.
Each was rewritten so that it reads A and works within strata of Y (Table 2, formulas in Appendix A).
text.formatted: Each was rewritten so that it reads A and works within strata of Y (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">2</ref>, formulas in Appendix A).

text.text: Within each Y stratum, the statistical detector tests every dimension for a group difference with Mann-Whitney or Kruskal-Wallis tests, and its score is the fraction of dimensions that stay significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction.
The geometric score is the distance between group centroids relative to the pooled withingroup spread, averaged over Y strata.
For bias direction PCA [35], samples are projected on the first principal direction of the group-mean differences within each stratum, and the score is the standardised gap of the projections.
text.formatted: For bias direction PCA <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref>, samples are projected on the first principal direction of the group-mean differences within each stratum, and the score is the standardised gap of the projections.

text.text: HBAC [44, 52] runs k-means (k = 8) on E within each stratum and scores the normalised mutual information between clusters and A. The frequency detector keeps only the top 5% of dimensions, ranked by their group difference on the training folds, and reports the conditional probe AUROC on those [53].
text.formatted: HBAC <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">[44,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">52]</ref> runs k-means (k = 8) on E within each stratum and scores the normalised mutual information between clusters and A. The frequency detector keeps only the top 5% of dimensions, ranked by their group difference on the training folds, and reports the conditional probe AUROC on those <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">[53]</ref>.

text.text: For descriptive purposes we also count how many detectors are flagged in a cell, k = 1[p probe < 0.05] + where p probe is the permutation p-value of the conditional probe, S is the set of the five secondary detectors (|S| = 5), q m is the Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value of secondary detector m computed across those five, and 1[•] is the indicator function, equal to 1 when its argument is true and 0 otherwise.
text.formatted: For descriptive purposes we also count how many detectors are flagged in a cell, k = 1[p probe < 0.05] + where p probe is the permutation p-value of the conditional probe, S is the set of the five secondary detectors (|S| = 5), q m is the Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value of secondary detector m computed across those five, and 1[•] is the indicator function, equal to 1 when its argument is true and 0 otherwise.

text.text: Decisions rest on the conditional probe alone, judged at the conventional level p < 0.05, and the count is reported as a description.
text.formatted: Decisions rest on the conditional probe alone, judged at the conventional level p < 0.05, and the count is reported as a description.

text.text: The secondary detectors are adjusted among themselves so that their flags share one false discovery level without touching the primary decision.
With K = 500 the smallest attainable p-value is 1/(K + 1) (and 1/(200 + 1) for the secondary statistics), and tables print the unadjusted p.
Section 5.2 reports how often the probe was significant and the one cell on which adjusting it with the secondary detectors would change the decision.

Because the detectors measure related properties of the same embedding, their flags are correlated, and Section 5.1 reports that correlation and the operating characteristics of every threshold k = 1, . . . , 6.
The package implements 20 methods.
Six of them, the six calibrated detectors in Table 2, need only (E, A, Y ) and are therefore usable when the encoder is a black box or an API that returns embeddings.
text.formatted: Six of them, the six calibrated detectors in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">2</ref>, need only (E, A, Y ) and are therefore usable when the encoder is a black box or an API that returns embeddings.

text.text: The other 14 need something an embedding audit does not have: a trained classifier, training dynamics, concept examples, images and model gradients, or an auxiliary model.
We kept them because they are useful when the user has the full model and training data, and because several are standard baselines.
Appendix B lists each with what it needs, and none contributes to any result in this paper except the group gaps computed for the heads of Section 4.3.
The package includes six mitigation methods (Appendix C).
Four of them work on frozen embeddings and are evaluated here with the package defaults.

Adversarial and contrastive debiasing pass the embeddings through a small learned debiasing network, which can change the audit score by itself, so each is compared with a control: the same network trained the same way with the adversarial or contrastive term switched off (for the contrastive method the task loss then has weight 1 instead of 0.25).

Shortcut masking sets to zero the 5% of embedding dimensions with the largest weight on the attribute direction, the difference between the group means of A after centring within Y , estimated on the training split.
Its control sets to zero the same number of randomly chosen dimensions.

Last-layer retraining (DFR) [54] leaves the embedding unchanged and refits the head on a training subset balanced over the four (A, Y ) groups, so its audit score cannot change and only the head is compared.
text.formatted: Last-layer retraining (DFR) <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[54]</ref> leaves the embedding unchanged and refits the head on a training subset balanced over the four (A, Y ) groups, so its audit score cannot change and only the head is compared.

text.text: Each method is run with 3 seeds.

For each method and control, the head is retrained on the transformed training embeddings and the audit is rerun on the transformed test-half embeddings, and both the audit score and the task AUROC are reported, so that removal of attribute information can be weighed against loss of task information.
Each detector implements detect(E, Y, A) → s m , and the calibration layer wraps any such function, so a new statistic inherits the permutation null without further work.
The audit is embedding-agnostic in the sense that any fixed-length vector with task and attribute labels can be passed to it, but only chest radiograph and face image embeddings were tested here.

The audit addresses the first question of the Introduction, and the head experiment takes up the second.
pip from its repository.
One command per dataset reruns the audit and the head experiment and then the table and figure scripts.
Every run writes a manifest that records the code commit and configuration together with hashes of the data (Appendix D).
The probe audit of 50,000 images with K = 500 permutations took 11 min on a laptop CPU.

The synthetic benchmark addresses the first question of the Introduction on data where the truth is known: it checks that the probe and the secondary detectors hold their false positive rate, and it measures their power.
The clinical audits then apply the test to common frozen encoders on two chest radiograph cohorts, for sex, age and race.

The classification-head experiment addresses the second question: it trains heads on confounded CheXpert data and asks whether the audit score predicts how much they rely on the attribute, and whether four mitigation methods reduce that reliance.
A planted image marker supplies a shortcut with known ground truth, and CelebA is a non-medical check.
Table 3 lists which method is used in which experiment.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">3</ref> lists which method is used in which experiment.

text.text: Seeds and run manifests are described in Appendix D.
The synthetic data make the answer known.
The task label is Y ∼ Bernoulli(0.5) and the attribute satisfies P (A = Y ) = ρ for ρ equal to 0.5, 0.7 or 0.9, so A and Y are distinct variables whose correlation we control.
Embeddings have d standard normal dimensions.
The task signal sits in its own block of dimensions.
The attribute signal sits in a separate block and comes in three forms.
In the linear mean shift the two groups differ by exactly δ standard deviations (each shifted by ±δ/2, so δ is Cohen's d in each attribute dimension).
The nonlinear XOR form leaves both group means at zero and carries the attribute in the sign of the product of two dimensions.
Under the variance shift the groups have equal means and unequal variances (Appendix E).
We varied δ ∈ {0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 1.2, 2.0}, n ∈ {200, 1000} and d ∈ {128, 512}, with 10 seeds per configuration.
The ground truth is that I(E; A | Y ) > 0 exactly when δ > 0.
text.formatted: The ground truth is that I(E; A | Y ) > 0 exactly when δ > 0.

text.text: At δ = 0 with ρ = 0.9, the embedding predicts A through Y but carries no extra information, which is the case a conditional test has to get right.
A mean shift in a few dimensions is a simplification.
Shortcut signal in real encoders is likely spread across many dimensions and may be nonlinear.

The XOR and variance variants were added to test whether each detector can see signals that leave group means unchanged, and the planted image marker (Section 4.3) tests the pipeline on a shortcut that passes through a real encoder.

For each detector and variant we report sensitivity (flag rate at δ > 0) and specificity (one minus flag rate at δ = 0), the operating characteristics of the descriptive count k for k = 1, . . . , 6, the pairwise correlation of detector flags, and the effective number of independent detectors computed from the eigenvalues of that correlation matrix [55, 56].
text.formatted: For each detector and variant we report sensitivity (flag rate at δ > 0) and specificity (one minus flag rate at δ = 0), the operating characteristics of the descriptive count k for k = 1, . . . , 6, the pairwise correlation of detector flags, and the effective number of independent detectors computed from the eigenvalues of that correlation matrix <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[55,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">56]</ref>.

text.text: We used the first 2,000 images streamed from a public Hugging Face mirror of the CheXpert training set [57].
text.formatted: We used the first 2,000 images streamed from a public Hugging Face mirror of the CheXpert training set <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">[57]</ref>.

text.text: These follow the order of the official train.csv, which is not random.
They come from 477 patients, and 423 are lateral views.

The mirror itself has no patient identifiers, so we joined each image by its path to the official train.csv, which gives the patient identifier, sex, age, view and findings, and took race per patient from the CheXpert demographics file.
Images without a demographics record, or with race recorded as unknown or refused (217 images), are left out of the race analyses.
Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander (24 images) is its own group and counts as non-White in the binary split.
All cross-validation and permutation on CheXpert is grouped by patient.
The audit task is Pneumothorax, with Y = 1 for a positive label and Y = 0 otherwise (prevalence 10.9%).
Y = 0 covers 584 negative, 23 uncertain and 1,175 blank labels, and Table F.7 repeats the audit on the 802 images with a definite label.
We used 1,491 subjects from MIMIC-CXR [58], one image per subject, so ordinary cross-validation is already patient-level.
text.formatted: We used 1,491 subjects from MIMIC-CXR <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">[58]</ref>, one image per subject, so ordinary cross-validation is already patient-level.

text.text: The images are a coreset of 1,999 images drawn for an earlier embedding project by stratified sampling on pathology labels (strategy "PathologyStratified-Clean", seed 0, of the public embedding dataset https://huggingface.co/datasets/MITCriticalData/qml-mimic-cxr-embeddings, which also provides the coreset strata used in [59]).
text.formatted: The images are a coreset of 1,999 images drawn for an earlier embedding project by stratified sampling on pathology labels (strategy "PathologyStratified-Clean", seed 0, of the public embedding dataset <ref type="url" target="https://huggingface.co/datasets/MITCriticalData/qml-mimic-cxr-embeddings">https://huggingface.co/  datasets/MITCriticalData/qml-mimic-cxr-embeddings</ref>, which also provides the coreset strata used in <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">[59]</ref>).

text.text: All are frontal (AP or PA) views.
Rows without a linked hospital admission outcome were removed.
The task is in-hospital mortality of the linked admission (hospital_expire_flag in MIMIC-IV [60]), prevalence 6.0%.
text.formatted: The task is in-hospital mortality of the linked admission (hospital_expire_flag in MIMIC-IV <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">[60]</ref>), prevalence 6.0%.

text.text: Mortality is an outcome that depends on many factors outside the image, and no radiological finding defines it.
All encoders were used frozen, with their published weights and no fine-tuning on either cohort.
Table 4 separates architecture from pretraining.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">4</ref> separates architecture from pretraining.

text.text: Some public encoders were pretrained on corpora that include CheXpert or MIMIC-CXR images.
RAD-DINO [61] publishes its list of training images, and all 2000 CheXpert images in our sample (477 patients) and 1479 of the 1491 MIMIC-CXR images are on it.
text.formatted: RAD-DINO <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">[61]</ref> publishes its list of training images, and all 2000 CheXpert images in our sample (477 patients) and 1479 of the 1491 MIMIC-CXR images are on it.

text.text: RAD-DINO is self-supervised, so it saw these images without their labels or attributes, and its scores here describe an encoder that has seen the audited images.
We did not train any encoder, so no patient in our analysis was used in a training step we controlled.
All seven CheXpert embeddings are extracted with code in the repository from pinned public checkpoints.
In the first submission four of them (ViT-B/32, DINOv2, RAD-DINO, MedSigLIP) were arrays stored without their extraction code, which could not be reproduced exactly.
We re-extracted those four from the same images, and every CheXpert result here uses the re-extracted arrays.
The extraction code reproduces the stored ViT-B/16 array, whose code was kept, to cosine 1.000, and Table F.6 compares the old and new arrays for the other four.
The MIMIC-CXR embeddings come from the same public dataset: the CLS token of ViT-Base-Patch16-224 and ViT-Base-Patch32-224, RAD-DINO, and MedSigLIP-448.

The dataset's documentation names google/siglip-so400m-patch14-384 for the last one, but re-embedding 50 of its images with google/medsiglip-448 reproduced the stored vectors (cosine 1.000 for every image), while the general-purpose SigLIP So400m checkpoint did not (median 0.15).

The audit measures potential, and to measure use and harm we trained classification heads on frozen CheXpert embeddings, for every encoder, with A equal to sex and then age, and three tasks: Pneumothorax, Pleural Effusion and Cardiomegaly.
For these tasks, uncertain and blank labels are dropped per task.
Train and test sets are disjoint at patient level (a two-fold split grouped by patient and stratified on (A, Y )), and each cell is repeated with 10 seeds.

Reliance on A is measured two ways: the gaps in true and false positive rate between groups on the test set, and the drop in test AUROC relative to a head trained on an unconfounded subsample of the same size.
We also report the mean absolute change in the head's output when the attribute direction is removed from the test embeddings (output shift).
Appendix C explains why it is not used as a measure of reliance.
That direction is the difference of the two group means after centring each Y stratum, estimated on the training pool.
Each test embedding x is replaced by x-((x-m) ⊤ u) u, with u the unit direction and m the training mean, and the confounded head is applied again.
We also report the head's AUROC separately on test images where A and Y agree with the training correlation (aligned) and where they disagree (misaligned), as in Kina and Petersen [14].
text.formatted: We also report the head's AUROC separately on test images where A and Y agree with the training correlation (aligned) and where they disagree (misaligned), as in Kina and Petersen <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: To check that the result does not depend on the linear head, the reliance measures are repeated on the same splits and seeds with a multilayer perceptron at the scikit-learn defaults (one hidden layer of 256 ReLU units, Adam with learning rate 10 -3 , L2 weight 10 -3 and up to 500 iterations).
Audit score against reliance.

Across encoder, attribute and task cells we compute the Spearman rank correlation between the conditional probe score, computed on all labelled images of the task, and each reliance measure, with a bootstrap confidence interval over cells.
The cells are not independent, since the seven encoders embed the same images and the attributes and tasks reuse the same patients.
We therefore also report an interval from resampling whole encoders and the partial correlation given attribute and task.
With seven encoders this interval is itself imprecise.

The three embedding-level mitigations of Section 3.6 and their controls are fitted on the confounded training embeddings and applied to the training and test embeddings, after which the head is retrained and the audit rerun on the test half of the patients.
For DFR only the head is refit.
Because the test half is smaller, the probe score before mitigation is lower than in Table 8, which uses all labelled images.

text.text: The TPR gap before mitigation is the mean over the first 3 of the 10 seeds.

Planted marker.

To test the pipeline on a shortcut with known ground truth that passes through a real encoder, we stamped a white square (27 by 27 pixels, intensity 255, at the same position on every image, its corner at 30% of the width and height) into the CheXpert images at 320 pixels on the shorter side, before the encoder's resizing to 224, embedded the images with the torchvision ResNet-50, and audited with the marker as the attribute and Pneumothorax as the task.
For the audit, images with Y = 1 received the marker at rate r = 0.5.
For the head, the training images with Y = 1 received it at rate 0.9.
Images with Y = 0 never carried the marker in training.
Patients were split in half for the head, and test images received the marker on a random half regardless of Y , so a head that ignores the marker shows no gap.
The experiment was repeated with 10 seeds.
CelebA [62] was used as a non-medical check.

text.text: We extracted ResNet-50 embeddings (2,048 dimensions) from 10,000 images drawn at random with a fixed seed from the 202,599 and audited A = Male given each of three tasks, Y ∈ {Blond hair, Heavy makeup, Attractive}, which are known to correlate with Male in this dataset.
Images are grouped by celebrity identity for crossvalidation and permutation.

text.text: The conditional permutation null held its nominal level.

Pooled over all null configurations, the detectors rejected in 0.02 (conditional probe) to 0.08 (bias direction) of runs at p < 0.05, the level at which the probe is judged, and after Benjamini-Hochberg across the five secondary detectors no secondary detector exceeded 0.03 (Table E.1).

text.text: The grid has 40 null data sets for each ρ, and at ρ = 0.9 the geometric and statistical detectors rejected in 0.17 and 0.12 of them, and the bias-direction detector in 0.15.
A permutation test is exact under H 0 whatever the statistic, so we drew 500 further null data sets at ρ = 0.9, n = 1000 and d = 128, the grid setting with the most rejections.
There the three rates were 0.05, 0.03 and 0.06 (HBAC 0.07, frequency 0.04, probe 0.03), so the higher grid values reflect how few grid data sets there are.
Conditioning mattered most when A and Y were strongly correlated.
At ρ = 0.9 and δ = 0, where the embedding predicts A only through Y , an unconditional probe rejected the null in 0.95 of data sets and the conditional probe in 0.03.
For the linear signal, the probe's sensitivity was 0.16 at δ = 0.2, 0.62 at δ = 0.5 and 0.87 at δ = 0.8 (Table 5, Figure 2).

text.text: The frequency, statistical and geometric detectors had similar power, and HBAC had much less.
Every detector missed the nonlinear and variance-shift signals.
At δ = 2.0 on the XOR variant, sensitivity was 0.02 for the probe, 0.02 for HBAC and 0.03 for the statistical detector, and on the variance-shift variant the same three were 0.02, 0.02 and 0.02.
For every detector and every δ, sensitivity on these two variants stayed at or near the level of its false positive rate under the null.
All six statistics respond to differences in group means, directly or through a linear model, and neither variant changes the means.

With patient-level permutation and folds grouped by patient, the probe rejected in 0.00 of draws (0 of 30; the 95% upper bound on its false positive rate is 0.11, so the control rules out the leakage rather than estimating that rate precisely).
All CheXpert re-    sults below use the patient-level version.

For sex on ResNet-50, for example, the AUROC was 0.841 grouped vs 0.887 plain.

The conditional probe rejected H 0 in 21 of 21 CheXpert cells and in 12 of 12 MIMIC-CXR cells.
Adjusting the probe's p-values across the 21 CheXpert cells by Benjamini-Hochberg leaves all 21 below 0.05 (largest q = 0.022), and the same holds across the 12 MIMIC-CXR cells.
The MIMIC-CXR ViT-B/32 row uses the file rebuilt from the source (Table F.5 and the comparison with the submitted pipeline below).
Sex had the largest potential, with a conditional probe AUROC of 0.84 to 0.99 on CheXpert and 0.93 to 1.00 on MIMIC-CXR, where RAD-DINO reached 1.00 (95% CI 1.00 to 1.00).
For age the ranges were 0.67 to 0.83 on CheXpert and 0.80 to 0.89 on MIMIC-CXR.

Race differed between the cohorts: 0.57 to 0.61 on CheXpert, where the MedSigLIP cell was the weakest and is flagged by the primary test alone (p = 0.022, none of its five secondary detectors flagged).
Had the probe been adjusted together with the secondary detectors, it would not have been (q = 0.13), and this is the only cell on which the two rules differ.
Race potential was higher at 0.66 to 0.76 on MIMIC-CXR.
MedSigLIP-448, re-extracted for this revision, was among the strongest CheXpert encoders for sex and age (0.97 and 0.80).
The unidentified array used under that name in the first submission had been the weakest for every attribute.
Table F.8 subsamples the non-White group to fixed sizes on RAD-DINO, ten draws per size.
On CheXpert the probe rejected in 0.10 of draws with 25 non-White images and in 0.80 with 400, and its AUROC varied widely between draws (SD 0.16 at the smallest size).
On MIMIC-CXR the rejection rate was 0.80 at 25 images and 1.00 at 400.

The CheXpert race signal is weak: the probe rejected in 7 of 10 draws with 200 non-White images and in 8 of 10 with 400, but rarely with 100 or fewer, whereas the MIMIC-CXR signal is detected with 50.

Keeping race groups with at least 50 images as separate groups (White, Black and Asian on CheXpert, and White and Black on MIMIC-CXR, which has 38 Asian subjects) gave somewhat higher AUROCs than the binary split (Table F.1), and four age bins gave somewhat lower ones than the binary split (Table F.2).
Table F.7 repeats the CheXpert probe with three changes.
On the 1577 frontal images alone no AUROC moved by more than 0.03, and 21 of 21 cells were significant, against 21 in the main audit.

Keeping only the 802 images with a definite Pneumothorax label, as in the head experiment, no AUROC moved by more than 0.06, and 20 of 21 cells had p < 0.05, with MedSigLIP race, the weakest cell of the main audit, the one exception.

With the arrays used in the first submission the four re-extracted encoders gave AUROCs up to 0.29 away from the main result, almost all of it from the unidentified MedSigLIP array.
Appending the squared coordinates to the probe's features changed the decision in 0 of 33 clinical cells and raised the AUROC by at most 0.02 (Appendix E, Table E.4).
To see whether the embeddings carry structure that the named attributes do not explain, we compared k-means clusters (k = 8) with all recorded metadata (Table F.9).

On both cohorts the clusters followed image acquisition most closely: the strongest association on CheXpert was with AP/PA and on MIMIC-CXR with view (AP/PA), and on CheXpert the frontal-versus-lateral view had a mean normalised mutual information of 0.378 with the clusters.
Support devices came next on CheXpert (0.068, range 0.052 to 0.103).

Sex, age and race were weakly associated with the clusters even where the probe recovered them well, so these attributes are encoded in directions that do not dominate the overall structure of the embedding.
Rerunning the submitted 13-method pipeline with only the flag reader fixed changed its clinical tables (Table F.10).

The statistical, geometric and GCE detectors, which the submitted tables showed as never flagging, flagged in every CheXpert cell once their results were read correctly, and the mean agreement count on CheXpert rose from 7.0 to 9.4 of 13 (MIMIC-CXR: 5.2 to 7.5).
The identical age and race rows of the submitted CheXpert table, present for 6 of 7 encoders, came from detectors that fitted on the task label and so returned the same output for every attribute.
These comparisons describe the old pipeline only, and none of its outputs is used elsewhere in this paper.

The submitted MIMIC-CXR ViT-B/32 file failed two independent checks (Table F.5): it held the first 1,491 rows of its source, taken before rows without an outcome were removed.
Its similarity structure matched no other encoder (largest Spearman correlation 0.006), and its sex probe was at chance (AUROC 0.50, against 0.93 for ViT-B/16 on the same images).
The file rebuilt from the source passed both (0.499 and 0.94), and every MIMIC-CXR result in this paper uses it.

With the mean of the permutation null subtracted from each probe score, which removes the part a head could get from Y alone, the correlation was 0.57 (0.75 within sex, 0.09 within age).

With a multilayer perceptron head (one hidden layer of 256 units) trained on the same splits the correlation was 0.53 (interval 0.20 to 0.76 when encoders are resampled), 0.70 within sex and 0.09 within age, and the two heads' TPR gaps correlated at 0.96 across cells.

With race as the attribute (White against non-White), the probe AU-ROCs spanned only 0.52 to 0.65, the confounded heads showed no consistent gap, and the correlation across the 21 cells was 0.03 (Table C.2 in Appendix C).

With adversarial debiasing the mean conditional probe AUROC changed by -0.09, and the number of audits with a significant probe went from 123 to 100 of 126.
The control network without the adversary changed it by -0.09, which leaves -0.01 for the adversary itself.
The contrastive debiasing method lowered the probe further, a change of -0.16 against -0.12 for its control, a difference of -0.04.
Significant audits went from 123 to 70, and to 85 for its control.
Relative to their controls, the adversarial and contrastive methods changed the task AUROC by 0.00 and 0.00 and the confounded head's TPR gap by -0.01 and 0.00.
Most of the lower audit score came from passing the embeddings through a small learned debiasing network, and in every case the confounded head found the attribute signal that remained.

Masking the top 5% of attribute dimensions barely moved the probe (-0.01, against 0.00 for random dimensions), because the attribute is spread over many dimensions, and relative to its control it changed the TPR gap by -0.01.
Refitting the head on a group-balanced subset was the only method that lowered the gap, from 0.18 to 0.01 on average and in 39 of 42 cells (Wilcoxon signed-rank test on cell means, p < 0.001).

text.text: The answer to the second question is partial: on CheXpert, encoders with higher conditional probe scores produced heads with larger subgroup gaps when the training data were confounded, with a rank correlation of 0.60 (interval 0.31 to 0.80 when whole encoders are resampled).
Within attributes the relation was strong for sex (0.74) and weak for age (0.19).

One reason is range restriction: the mean TPR gap of the age cells varied little between cells (SD 0.05, against 0.10 for sex) while seeds within a cell varied by 0.14, so the ranking of age cells is largely seed noise.
For a linear head trained on confounded data, shortcut potential measured on the embedding was therefore informative about use, clearly for sex, not significantly for age.
For race, whose potential on CheXpert was weak for every encoder, the heads showed no consistent gap and the relation was not detectable over that range (0.03, Appendix C).
It does not establish use.

The correlation is across cells, and it was measured for logistic and small MLP heads under one form of confounding, on training sets of 42 to 272 images drawn from a CheXpert sample that is not random.
A head trained on unconfounded data showed almost no gap between aligned and misaligned images on the same embeddings.
Whether an attribute is used depends on the training data and the head, as Brown et al. [10], Petersen et al. [13] and Kina and Petersen [14] argue.
text.formatted: Whether an attribute is used depends on the training data and the head, as Brown et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>, Petersen et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> and Kina and Petersen <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> argue.

text.text: Our aligned and misaligned AUROCs repeat the pattern Kina and Petersen found for a chest-drain shortcut on frozen foundation models.

The mitigation results add a caution: at the package defaults, adversarial and contrastive debiasing lowered the conditional probe score, but the same debiasing networks trained without the mitigation term lowered it nearly as much (for contrastive debiasing the difference from its control was -0.04), and masking the top attribute dimensions did little more than masking random ones.
None of the three moved the confounded head's TPR gap by more than 0.01 beyond its control.
A head trained on confounded data found the attribute signal that remained.
The one method that closed the gap, refitting the head on group-balanced data, left the embedding and its audit score unchanged and cost task AUROC, for reasons unrelated to balancing (Appendix C).
Both observations agree with the view that much of shortcut use on frozen encoders is decided in the head [14], and with MEDFAIR's finding that mitigation often does not beat plain training [46].
text.formatted: Both observations agree with the view that much of shortcut use on frozen encoders is decided in the head <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>, and with MEDFAIR's finding that mitigation often does not beat plain training <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[46]</ref>.

text.text: An audit score can fall for reasons that have nothing to do with debiasing, so a mitigation needs a control, and the head has to be tested.
A positive audit for general-purpose encoders is unsurprising, since encoders pretrained on large image corpora are built to retain most of what is visible.

Sex and age leave visible traces in chest radiographs, and earlier work recovered race from chest radiographs, which radiologists cannot do [8, 11], and sex, site and scanner from knee radiographs almost perfectly [12].

text.text: For sex in particular, part of the signal is likely anatomical.
The audit cannot separate legitimate anatomical information from unwanted information, because both are information about A given Y .
Subgroup separability sets an upper limit on harm without implying it [32], and the audit should be read in that sense.

text.text: Our probe results agree in direction with the encoding of sex, age and race reported by Gichoya et al. and Glocker et al. on full chest X-ray models [8, 11], though our numbers are not directly comparable, because we audit frozen embeddings on small samples and condition on a task.

text.text: Calibrated by permutation, the same idea also works as a check on a frozen encoder.

On this evidence they add very little: their flags rose and fell with the probe's as the effect size changed (effective number 1.5 of 6 over the whole grid, 2.2 at a fixed δ = 0.5), and requiring several of them to agree only cost sensitivity.
None of them detected the XOR or variance-shift signals that the probe missed.
In the submitted version we read disagreement between detectors as evidence about the geometry of the encoding.
Most of that disagreement came from code faults, and the remainder is explained by differences in power.

Combining detectors resembles ensembling [63] or a mixture of experts [64], but ensembles gain from roughly independent errors, which these detectors have only in part, and a mixture of experts would need a gate trained on labelled shortcuts.

text.text: We keep the secondary detectors as diagnostics because their scores are on interpretable scales (fraction of dimensions, centroid distance), and they play no part in the decision.
Race potential was weak on CheXpert and clearer on MIMIC-CXR.
The cohorts differ in task and sampling, and in the make-up of the non-White group, so we do not read this as an institution effect.

The clusters followed view and projection on both cohorts, consistent with earlier reports that hospital [6] and scanner [7] signals, and site signals in knee radiographs [12], dominate what image models pick up.
text.formatted: The clusters followed view and projection on both cohorts, consistent with earlier reports that hospital <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> and scanner <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> signals, and site signals in knee radiographs <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>, dominate what image models pick up.

text.text: Several of the problems we found were data-handling faults.
Repeated images of one patient made every detector reject a meaningless attribute until permutation and folds were grouped by patient.
One MIMIC-CXR embedding file did not match its metadata, and the submitted tables reported shortcut flags for it.
The CheXpert sex column was inverted in the submitted runs.
The first two can be caught cheaply, with a fake-attribute control and a row-alignment check, and we recommend running them before any audit.
The audit, and every secondary detector, missed the two attribute signals we tested that leave group means unchanged: on the XOR and variance-shift variants no detector did better than chance.

The gap lies in the statistics, which are built around differences in location: under the same permutation null, probes on squared coordinates and on pairwise products detected both signals with their calibration intact (Appendix E), and on the clinical cohorts the squared-feature probe changed no decision (Table E.4).
A linear probe was a deliberate choice, since it matches how frozen embeddings are usually used, but a nonlinear head could exploit signal that the audit reports as absent.
A negative audit is therefore weaker evidence than a positive one.
The audit needs labelled sensitive attributes, which are often missing or recorded as imperfect proxies.
It examines one embedding at a time, from one layer of one encoder, and says nothing about other layers or about the encoder after fine-tuning.
For age the score was not significantly related to reliance, so on this cohort the audit met its own usefulness criterion clearly for sex only.

The head experiment covers two head types (logistic regression and a small multilayer perceptron) and one form of confounding, with two attributes (race, whose signal on CheXpert is weak, only as an additional run in Table C.2) and three tasks on one cohort, and the correlation between audit and reliance is computed across only 42 cells that share encoders.

text.text: With seven encoders, the interval that resamples them is coarse.
The heads pool frontal and lateral views, and on frontal views alone the audit AUROCs moved by at most 0.03.

The CheXpert sample is the first 2,000 images in the order of the official training file, not a random sample, so the CheXpert results may not hold for the full training set and may carry whatever ordering the file was assembled with.

Against the full training file the sample has a similar sex and race mix (43% against 41% female, and 64.5% against 63.8% White among images with a recorded race) and slightly younger patients (median age 59 against 62).
It also has more lateral views (21% against 14%), which the frontal-only analysis bounds.
The MIMIC-CXR task, in-hospital mortality, is an outcome with many causes outside the image.
MIMIC-CXR also has radiological labels, which we did not use as tasks, and the audit's result is specific to the task it conditions on.
Both samples are small, which limits power for small groups.
The CheXpert race result in particular is rarely detected with 100 or fewer non-White images.
Collapsing race into White against non-White hides differences between groups.
Records with race unknown, declined or not obtained are left out on both cohorts (217 CheXpert images, 71 MIMIC-CXR subjects).
The head-experiment cells are not independent and some are small (42 to 272 training and 60 to 404 test images).
The identity of the MIMIC-CXR encoders could not be verified from code.
On CheXpert the four re-extracted encoders replaced arrays whose origin is unknown, and the old and new arrays differ (Table F.6).
RAD-DINO was pretrained on nearly all the images audited here, and for the other encoders the pretraining data could not be checked image by image.

MedSigLIP was trained on medical images paired with reports, MIMIC-CXR among them, so its text side could have taught it findings and demographics that reports mention, and its MIMIC-CXR scores, like RAD-DINO's, may describe an encoder that saw the audited images in pretraining.
CheXpert is not among the public data sets its model card lists, and the card does not itemise its licensed data sets.

The Benjamini-Hochberg correction is applied across the five secondary detectors within each cell, and the primary probe is judged at p < 0.05 in each cell, with no adjustment across cells for either.
text.formatted: The Benjamini-Hochberg correction is applied across the five secondary detectors within each cell, and the primary probe is judged at p < 0.05 in each cell, with no adjustment across cells for either.

text.text: SIS was removed from the score, and methods that need training access were not evaluated.

We compared embedding clusters with recorded metadata but did not run an error-aware slice discovery method such as GEORGE or Domino [42, 43], so subgroups on which a head fails without a recorded attribute were not searched for.
text.formatted: We compared embedding clusters with recorded metadata but did not run an error-aware slice discovery method such as GEORGE or Domino <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43]</ref>, so subgroups on which a head fails without a recorded attribute were not searched for.

text.text: The mitigations were run only on CheXpert and only at the package defaults, without tuning, so tuned settings could change the result, and the planted marker is a single, simple artefact on one encoder.

We asked whether shortcut potential can be measured on a frozen embedding, and whether the measurement predicts how strongly a head trained on that embedding with confounded data relies on the attribute.

ShortKit-ML measures the shortcut potential of a frozen embedding for a task with one primary test, a conditional probe calibrated by permuting the attribute within task strata and, where a patient has several images, between patients.

The test held its error rate on synthetic data and found a planted marker in every seed, but like every detector here it missed signals that leave group means unchanged, so a negative audit does not rule out a shortcut that a nonlinear head could use.

On CheXpert, its score correlated with how strongly a logistic head trained on confounded data relied on the attribute (Spearman 0.60, 0.74 within sex, not significant within age), but at the package defaults three embedding-level mitigations did no better than their controls at reducing that reliance.
Refitting the head on a group-balanced subset closed that gap, in 39 of 42 cells, without changing the audit score.
Task AUROC fell because that subset was small and because the package's DFR head uses an L1 penalty.
The audit is a first check on an encoder, and the head trained on it has to be tested as well.
Two cheap checks caught our own data faults and belong before any audit: a fake patient-level attribute that no detector should find, and a row-alignment check between encoders.
Three extensions would make the audit more useful.
Probes on squared and product features found the XOR and variance-shift signals that no detector here found (Appendix E).
Making such tests part of the audit, with product features at encoder dimension, is the next step, since on the clinical cohorts the squared probe changed no decision.
The link between audit score and reliance should be checked on other cohorts and with larger heads, and under confounding other than a single correlated attribute.
Auditing an encoder on images it was pretrained on and on images it never saw would show how much of the potential comes from the pretraining data.
The audit is intended as one of the embedding-level checks in DOJO, a community-driven platform for adversarial evaluation of health AI [65].
text.formatted: The audit is intended as one of the embedding-level checks in DOJO, a community-driven platform for adversarial evaluation of health AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">[65]</ref>.

text.text: The wider lesson is about what can be measured.
A shortcut can only be audited through an attribute someone recorded, and most of what an encoder has learned from its training data was never recorded.
This toolkit is a first step for the case where the attribute is known and the input is a frozen embedding.

The harder cases, confounders with no label, signals that no linear test sees, and inputs beyond embeddings (the image itself, text and multimodal encoders) need tools that do not yet exist, and we see this work as a map of which ones to build next. use agreements.

text.text: Settings used in the head experiment.

Adversarial debiasing uses a debiasing network (one linear layer to 64 units, with ReLU and dropout 0.1) followed by a linear task head and, behind a gradient-reversal layer (reversal weight 0.5), a linear adversary.
The loss is the sum of the task and adversary crossentropies, trained with Adam (learning rate 10 -3 , batch 64) for 50 epochs.
Contrastive debiasing uses the same network.

For each anchor it draws up to 32 positives (same Y , other A) and 32 negatives (other Y ), and minimises 0.75 times an InfoNCE loss (temperature 0.05, one term per positive against the negatives) plus 0.25 times the task cross-entropy, with Adam (learning rate 10 -3 ) for 50 epochs.
Their controls are the same networks trained on the task loss alone.
The contrastive loss in the released package was corrected during the revision: it had treated additional positives of an anchor as negatives.
The embedding passed on is the 64-unit output of that network.
Shortcut masking and its control are as defined in Section 3.6, applied to the training, test and audit embeddings.

DFR standardises the embedding and refits an L1 logistic head (C = 1, balanced class weights, and the L1 penalty follows the DFR reference implementation [54]) on a subset of the confounded training set with equal numbers of images in each of the four (A, Y ) groups, so it uses 4× the size of the smallest group.
text.formatted: DFR standardises the embedding and refits an L1 logistic head (C = 1, balanced class weights, and the L1 penalty follows the DFR reference implementation <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[54]</ref>) on a subset of the confounded training set with equal numbers of images in each of the four (A, Y ) groups, so it uses 4× the size of the smallest group.

text.text: To separate the effect of size from that of balancing, we refit the same L1 head on a random subset of the confounded training set of the same size, and an L2 head (as for the confounded head) on the balanced subset, over the same cells and seeds.

Task AUROC was 0.65 for DFR, 0.65 for the random subset of the same size, which kept a TPR gap of 0.10 (so the small subset alone removed about half of the confounded head's gap of 0.18), and 0.69 for the balanced subset with the L2 head, against 0.73 for the confounded head.
Balancing itself cost no AUROC.
The loss came from the small subset and the L1 penalty in about equal parts.
Output shift.
The output shift of Section 4.3 correlated negatively with the probe score (-0.26).
Projecting out u moves each test embedding by its whole coordinate along u, most of which is spread within each attribute group rather than the gap between groups.

The measure therefore tracks how much the head responds to that spread, which is largest for encoders that encode the attribute weakly, so it is reported in Table 8 but not used as a measure of reliance.

text.text: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
This study used three publicly available datasets: CheXpert, MIMIC-CXR, and CelebA.
CheXpert was released by the Stanford Machine Learning Group under a research data use agreement and consists of deidentified chest radiographs.
MIMIC-CXR was released by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Laboratory for Computational Physiology under the Phys-ioNet Credentialed Health Data License 1.5.0.
Access to MIMIC-CXR was obtained through completion of the required CITI Data or Specimens Only Research training (PhysioNet credentialed user).
CelebA is a publicly available facial attribute dataset released for academic research.
No new human subjects data were collected for this study.

As all data used had been collected and deidentified before their release through established public repositories under their respective data use agreements, this work did not require additional institutional review board approval.
The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.
During the preparation of this work the authors used Claude (Anthropic) in order to draft the first version of the manuscript and to review the code.
MIMIC-CXR data stayed on institutional machines and were not given to Claude or any other AI service, and model training on the authors' conversations was disabled.
After using this tool, the authors reviewed and edited the content as needed and take full responsibility for the content of the published article.
Notation: for each image i, E i ∈ R d is its standardised embedding, with attribute group a i and task label y i .
S y = {i : y i = y} is a task stratum and S y,a = {i : y i = y, a i = a} a cell.
Statistics averaged over strata are weighted by |S y |.
All six statistics are calibrated by the conditional permutation null of Section 3.2.
The null recomputes the whole statistic, including any fitted direction, ranking or clustering, on each permuted data set.
Conditional probe.
L2-regularised logistic regression on [E i , y i ], regularisation strength 1, 5-fold CV stratified on (a, y) and grouped by patient (CheXpert) or identity (CelebA), averaged over five fold splits.
Its statistic s is the out-of-fold AUROC for A (macro one-vs-rest when G > 2) [17, 18].

text.text: For each dimension j and stratum y, a Mann-Whitney U test (G = 2) or Kruskal-Wallis test (G > 2) of E ij across groups within S y .
text.formatted: For each dimension j and stratum y, a Mann-Whitney U test (G = 2) or Kruskal-Wallis test (G > 2) of E ij across groups within S y .

text.text: All d × |Y| p-values are adjusted by Benjamini-Hochberg at 0.05 [51], and s is the fraction of dimensions significant in at least one stratum.

text.text: Within stratum y, with group centroids µ y,a , the mean pairwise centroid distance over the pooled within-group spread.
The statistic s is the weighted mean of s y.
Within stratum y, v y is the first principal component of the group-mean differences (for G = 2, the normalised difference of the two means) [35].
text.formatted: Within stratum y, v y is the first principal component of the group-mean differences (for G = 2, the normalised difference of the two means) <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref>.

text.text: With projections z i = v ⊤ y E i , s y is the largest absolute difference of group means of z divided by the pooled standard deviation of z.
Because v y is fitted on the same data, s y is positive even under the null.
The permutation null accounts for this, which a fixed threshold did not.
